young.html: Edward Gibbon was a young Englishman visiting Rome in 1764. One evening, sitting among the ruins of the old Capitol, he heard friars singing in a church built on the spot where a temple once stood. He had an idea: he would write the story of how the mighty Roman Empire declined and fell.

It took him more than twenty years and six thick volumes! The first half tells how Rome was strong and peaceful under a few good emperors, around AD 100, and then had more and more trouble: bad rulers, soldiers choosing emperors, money problems and invasions.

Emperors tried to fix things. Constantine built a new capital, Constantinople, and became the first Christian emperor. But in the west, peoples like the Goths and Vandals crossed the borders, Rome itself was sacked in AD 410, and in AD 476 the last emperor in the west, a boy, was set aside.

young.html: Build and crumble. Build a tall tower of blocks or cups. Each person names one thing that kept Rome strong (roads, laws, the army, trade) and adds a block. Then name troubles (bad rulers, invasions, high taxes) and take a block away for each. When does the tower fall? Gibbon wondered why Rome lasted so long.

full.text: The great historian of the Enlightenment

full.html: Gibbon (1737–1794) published the first volume of The History of the Decline and Fall of the Roman Empire in 1776, the same year as Smith's Wealth of Nations and the Declaration of Independence; the last three volumes followed in 1788. Its 71 chapters run from the 2nd century AD to the 15th. Volume 37 of the set holds roughly the first half, from the Antonine emperors through the end of the empire in the west and the barbarian kingdoms that followed.

full.text: If a man were called to fix the period in the history of the world, during which the condition of the human race was most happy and prosperous, he would, without hesitation, name that which elapsed from the death of Domitian to the accession of Commodus. The vast extent of the Roman empire was governed by absolute power, under the guidance of virtue and wisdom.
full.author: Edward Gibbon
full.ed: The History of the Decline and Fall of the Roman Empire, with notes by H. H. Milman (Project Gutenberg text)

full.html: The "five good emperors" (Nerva, Trajan, Hadrian, Antoninus Pius and Marcus Aurelius, AD 96–180) ruled, Gibbon says, as if they were servants of the laws. But their goodness depended on the character of one man. Under Commodus (AD 180–192) and then in the 3rd century, the army made and unmade emperors, and civil war, plague and invasion followed.

full.text: Reform, a new capital and a new faith

full.html: Diocletian (284–305) divided the empire's rule and rebuilt its defenses. Constantine (306–337) won power, favored Christianity and founded Constantinople in 330. In chapters 15 and 16 Gibbon explains the spread of Christianity by what he calls secondary causes, such as the zeal and discipline of the early Christians, and argues that the number of martyrs had been exaggerated. Many readers in his day were angered; his defenders said he was writing as a historian looking for human causes, his critics that his irony showed contempt for the faith.

Gibbon tells of the emperor Julian's attempt to restore the old religion, the arrival of the Huns, the Gothic victory at Adrianople (378), Alaric's sack of Rome (410), Attila, and the Vandals in Africa. In 476 the general Odoacer deposed the young emperor Romulus Augustulus and did not name another. Gibbon then pauses to reflect:

full.text: But the decline of Rome was the natural and inevitable effect of immoderate greatness. Prosperity ripened the principle of decay; the causes of destruction multiplied with the extent of conquest; and as soon as time or accident had removed the artificial supports, the stupendous fabric yielded to the pressure of its own weight. The story of its ruin is simple and obvious; and instead of inquiring why the Roman empire was destroyed, we should rather be surprised that it had subsisted so long.

full.html: Gibbon's causes. In different places he points to the size of the empire, the power of the army, the loss of the old civic spirit, the division between east and west, the barbarian invasions and, controversially, the effect of Christianity and monasticism on public life. He gives no single cause.
Thinking the whole Roman Empire fell in 476. The eastern half, ruled from Constantinople, lasted almost a thousand years more; that is the story of the second half, on the next rung.

deep.html: Gibbon read the ancient sources with great care, and his footnotes are famous for their learning and wit. Modern historians have far more evidence, from archaeology, coins and inscriptions, and many prefer to speak of the "transformation" of the Roman world in late antiquity rather than simple decline, while others have argued that the fall in the west was real and brought a steep drop in living standards. Gibbon's view of Christianity's role is now widely judged one-sided. Yet his book is still read for its style and its sweep.

Compare the other histories on this ladder: Herodotus and Thucydides wrote of wars they lived near; Tacitus, whom Gibbon admired, wrote of the early empire; Augustine's City of God answered pagans who blamed Christianity for the sack of 410.

care: Gibbon describes wars, palace murders and persecutions, usually briefly and in a stately style. His famous chapters 15 and 16 on early Christianity are critical and were controversial; we summarize them fairly.
